newsitem.title: switzerland: UNHCR chief condemns Tajik kidnaps, attacks.
newsitem.headline: UNHCR chief condemns Tajik kidnaps, attacks.

text.p: Sadako Ogata, United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees, on Thursday condemned recent attacks against humanitarian workers including the kidnapping of four of her staff in Tajikistan.

In a statement in Geneva, Ogata called on the Tajik government to secure the immediate release of the four UNHCR staff members including a Nigerian expatriate, who were snatched by rebels in Tajikistan's capital Dushanbe early on Thursday.
She said that all the hostages had been taken to Obigarm, 80 km (50 miles) east of Dushanbe, "a stronghold of an armed opposition group believed responsible for the kidnappings".
The same Tajik rebels seized five U.N. observers, two International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) delegates and five journalists on Tuesday and on Wednesday.
The ICRC said it had suspended its work in the former Soviet republic after the kidnappings.
"We deplore the kidnappings in the strongest possible terms," said Ogata, who urged the Tajikistan government "to do its utmost in securing the immediate release of the hostages".

"The abductions of the UNHCR workers today took place in broad daylight in Dushanbe during regular working hours. They were being transported out of the city, past government checkpoints," Ogata said.
"The incident regrettably indicates the serious deterioration in the security situation for UNHCR and other international workers," she said.

In an interview with Reuters, Ogata later condemned attacks against aid workers in conflict zones around the world, including the killing of five United Nations human rights staff in Rwanda by unidentified gunmen on Tuesday.

"This is really very, very worrying. These things should not happen," said the former professor of international relations from Japan, calling for "strong determination by authorities and international insistence that humanitarian rules are respected."
"There is a lot of conflict going on in the world, a lot of law and order problems," Ogata said.
"Whenever there is a breakdown in security and order, people suffer and can't be protected by governments. We try to help. Humanitarian staff are at the forefront of today's conflicts."

The U.N. has lost more than 150 workers in conflicts since 1987, including 50 in Rwanda, said Raymonde Martineau, head of the U.N. staff association for security of aid workers. In 1996, the ICRC lost six staffers in Chechnya and three in Burundi.
